3.text: range ceremonials with details closely resembling some of those described.

4.text: Thus, in the Pacific Koryak and Kerek villages, the carcass of a killed fox

5.text: is brought into the house and deposited near the fire. The master says,

6.text: “Let the guest warm himself. When he feels warm, we will free him from

7.text: his overcoat.” In the mean time the placing of the carcass near the fire has

8.text: a very real purpose. As foxes are killed almost exclusively in winter, the

9.text: carcass is always frozen, and it must be thawed out before it can be skinned.

10.text: In due time the fox is skinned. Two broad strips of long, soft grass, which

11.text: grows on the seashore, are wrapped around the bare carcass. One strip

12.text: serves as a belt; the other, as a boa. The mouth of the carcass is filled
12.note: a small ink speck sits between 'belt' and ';' at 2x/4x zoom; it aligns with descenders bleeding through from the line above and is not ink on this line's own box.

13.text: with fish-eggs. The mistress gashes the flesh in several places, and puts

14.text: into the cuts more fish-eggs or dried meat, pretending that the cuts are

15.text: pockets of the fox, which she wants to fill with provisions. Then the carcass

16.text: is carried out of the house, and the people say, “Go and tell your friends

17.text: that it is good to visit yonder house. Instead of my old coat, they gave

18.text: me a new one still warmer and with longer hair. I have eaten my fill, and

19.text: had my pockets well stored. You, too, go and visit them.” It is believed

22.text: Jochelson² gives details of a ceremony among the Koryak of the Okhotsk

23.text: shore very similar to those relating to the fox-carcass. Steller³ mentions almost

24.text: identical practices among the Kamchadal. In the ceremonial arranged after

25.text: a successful hunt of the bear, when the bear-meat is cooked and eaten, the

26.text: master brings in the head of the bear, adorns it with grass, hangs around it

27.text: bits of various meats, and then asks the bear not to be angry with the

28.text: hunters, because the last stroke was given by the Russians. He also asks

29.text: him to inform his relatives of this, that they may come to the same place

31.text: Krasheninnikoff also mentions⁴ similar details in the Kamchadal ceremo-

32.text: nial of seal-heads. The heads, he says, are fed with pudding. A large

33.text: stone is deposited on the floor of the hut, which symbolizes the sea, and it

34.text: is surrounded with smaller ones, which represent the pebbles on the shore.

35.text: The seals are dragged upon these stones to give them an idea that it is very

36.text: agreeable to visit the Kamchadal huts, where even the sea is surrounded with

37.text: pebbles. In doing this, the people cry, “Come oftener! we feel dull without

38.text: you.” Krasheninnikoff also mentions⁵ that the natives of Alutora, in their

39.text: whale ceremonial, carry a wooden image of a whale to the seashore, exclaiming,

40.text: “The whale is gone to the sea!”
